title: Genesis 43. The Cup of Yielding.

phrases: Genesis 43. The Cup of Yielding.
The famine was severe in the land.
When they had eaten up the grain which they had brought out of Egypt,
their father said to them: Go again,
buy us a little more food.
The grain ran out.
The food from Egypt, the grain Joseph stored,
the grain Joseph sold them,
the grain that was placed in sacks with returned silver, is gone.
The Cup that was filled in chapter forty-two is now empty.
The testing has not ended.
The famine forces the issue.
Judah spoke to him, saying: The man solemnly warned us, saying:
You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.
If you will send our brother with us,
we will go down and buy you food.
But if you will not send him, we will not go down.
Not Reuben.
Judah.
The firstborn tried in chapter forty-two, offered his own sons as guarantee.
Jacob refused.
Now Judah, the one who sold Joseph,
the one who confessed she is more righteous than I,
the one who descended from his brothers and married a Canaanite and lost two sons and withheld the third,
steps forward.
The transfer point.
In chapter thirty-seven, Judah said sell him.
He offered his brother for profit.
In chapter thirty-eight,
Judah withheld his son Shelah from Tamar and was caught.
Now Judah offers himself as guarantee.
Send the boy with me, and we will get up and go,
so that we may live, and not die, both we, and you,
and also our little ones.
I myself will be collateral for him.
From my hand will you require him.
If I do not bring him to you and set him before you,
then let me bear the blame forever.
I will bear the blame forever.
the same word for sin.
If I fail, I sin, against you, forever.
The one who sold a brother now pledges his life for a brother.
The one who said what profit is it if we kill our brother now says:
I will be the guarantee.
The Cup of Judah's betrayal is being turned into a Cup of surety.
The betrayer becomes the guarantor.
This is the turning of Judah.
The covenant line, the line of Perez, the line of David,
the line that will lead to Christ,
passes through a man who sold his brother and then offered himself for a brother.
The Cup that traveled through the scandal of chapter thirty-eight, through Tamar,
through the seal and cord and staff,
through the confession she is more righteous than I,
now travels through a man who says:
let me bear the blame forever.
Israel their father said to them: If it must be so,
then do this.
Take from the choice fruits of the land in your bags,
and carry down a present for the man, a little balm,
a little honey, spices and myrrh, nuts, and almonds.
And take double money in your hand,
and take back the money that was returned in the mouth of your sacks.
Perhaps it was an oversight.
Take your brother also, get up, and return to the man.
Jacob yields.
The father who said all these things are against me now says:
if it must be so.
The Cup of fear yields to the Cup of surrender.
The same father who held Benjamin so tight he would not let him go now opens his hand.
The balm and honey and myrrh and nuts and almonds,
the fruits of the land that Jacob stole from his brother,
the land of Canaan,
are sent as a gift to the man who holds his son.
The father who was deceived sends gifts to the man he does not know is his son.
And then Jacob speaks the name: El Shaddai,
give you mercy before the man,
that he may release to you your other brother and Benjamin.
El Shaddai.
The name God used in chapter thirty-five when He confirmed Israel's name.
The name God used in chapter seventeen when He changed Abram to Abraham.
The name Isaac used when he blessed Jacob.
Jacob uses the covenant name, not as a complaint this time,
but as a blessing.
The man who said if at Bethel now says El Shaddai at home.
The conditional has become a prayer.
And as for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.
If I am bereaved, I am bereaved.
The same words Rebekah might have said when she sent Jacob away.
The father opens his hand.
The Cup of yielding, the last surrender before the reunion.
Jacob lets Benjamin go.
The father who could not let go of Rachel's last son releases him into the hands of the God whose name he just spoke.
El Shaddai.
God Almighty.
The name that was spoken at the covenant of circumcision.
The name that was spoken at Bethel.
The name that now covers a father's surrender.
The men took the present, and they took double money, and Benjamin.
They got up, went down to Egypt, and stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them,
he said to the steward of his house:
Bring the men into the house, and butcher an animal, and prepare,
for the men will dine with me at noon.
Joseph sees Benjamin.
The brother he has never met as a man.
The boy who was a child when Joseph was sold.
The son of his mother, Rachel,
who died on the road to Bethlehem,
who named her first son add and her second son,
son of my sorrow.
Joseph sees the living proof that Rachel's womb produced two sons,
and the second one is standing in front of him.
The men were afraid, because they were brought to Joseph's house.
They said:
Because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time,
we are brought in, that he may seek occasion against us,
attack us, and seize us as slaves, along with our donkeys.
The Cup of fear.
The brothers who carried guilt for twenty years now see provision as a trap.
The money that was returned,
the silver that was placed in their sacks by Joseph's command,
is now feared as evidence against them.
The brothers who said what is this that God has done to us?
now expect punishment.
The guilt that was silent has become a lens.
Everything that happens is interpreted through the Cup of fear.
They came near to the steward and spoke to him at the door:
Oh, my lord,
we indeed came down the first time to buy food.
When we came to the lodging place, we opened our sacks,
and behold, each man's money was in the mouth of his sack,
our money in full weight.
We have brought it back in our hand.
We have brought down other money to buy food.
We do not know who put our money in our sacks.
He said: Peace be to you.
Do not be afraid.
Your God and the God of your father has given you treasure in your sacks.
I received your money.
Peace.
The steward, a pagan servant in Joseph's house, speaks of God's provision.
Your God and the God of your father.
The man who serves Joseph knows something about Joseph's God.
The Cup of testing is being softened.
The steward does not say: it was my master's plan.
He says: your God did this.
The recognition of God's provision comes through the mouth of an Egyptian servant,
the same pattern as Potiphar recognizing the Lord was with Joseph.
He brought Simeon out to them.
Simeon.
Released.
The brother who was bound in chapter forty-two is now brought out.
The Cup of testing has held him, and now releases him.
The brothers who left him bound are now given him back.
The test is not over.
But the mercy is visible.
The man brought the men into Joseph's house, and gave them water,
and they washed their feet.
He gave their donkeys fodder.
They prepared the present for Joseph's coming at noon,
for they heard that they should eat bread there.
Washed feet.
Fed donkeys.
Prepared gifts.
The brothers who were in custody for three days are now treated as guests.
The Cup of testing is becoming the Cup of hospitality.
The men who expected slavery received washing.
When Joseph came home,
they brought him the present which was in their hand into the house,
and bowed themselves down to the earth before him.
Again.
The dream deepens.
The sheaves bow again.
The brothers who said: Will you indeed reign over us?
bow to the earth before the brother they sold.
He asked them of their welfare, and said: Is your father well,
the old man of whom you spoke?
Is he yet alive?
They said: Your servant, our father, is well.
He is still alive.
They bowed down humbly.
Joseph asks about the father who was deceived by the coat.
The father who wept and refused comfort.
The father who said:
I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning.
Is he still alive?
Yes.
The father who believed his son was dead is alive.
And the son who is asking is alive.
And neither knows about the other.
Then Joseph lifted up his eyes and saw Benjamin, his brother,
son of his mother, and said:
Is this your youngest brother of whom you spoke to me?
And he said: God be gracious to you, my son.
Son of his mother.
Joseph and Benjamin, the only two sons of Rachel.
The woman who said give me children, or I die.
The woman who named her firstborn add.
The woman who died giving birth to the second.
Joseph looks at the boy Rachel died for and says:
God be gracious to you, my son.
My son.
Not my brother, my son.
The word that a father uses.
Joseph, who has two sons of his own, Manasseh and Ephraim,
now looks at Benjamin and calls him my son.
The Cup that was held by a mother who died breaks open in a brother who weeps.
Joseph hurried, for his heart yearned over his brother.
He sought a place to weep.
He entered into his room and wept there.
The second weeping.
Chapter forty-two: he wept at hearing their guilt.
Chapter forty-three: he wept at seeing Benjamin.
The Cup of testing holds both,
the brothers' acknowledged sin and the brother who was never part of it.
Benjamin was a child when Joseph was sold.
Innocent in the betrayal.
And Joseph's tears break for the innocent one.
The brother who grew up without his brother.
The boy who never knew what happened to the older sibling who vanished.
The son of Rachel, the woman who died so he could live.
He washed his face and came out.
He controlled himself and said: Serve the meal.
He controls himself.
The man who weeps is also the man who governs.
The Cup of tears is poured in private.
The Cup of testing continues in public.
The brother who feels must also be the brother who tests.
Both at once.
They served him by himself, and them by themselves,
and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves,
because the Egyptians do not eat with the Hebrews,
for that is an abomination to the Egyptians.
The separation.
Hebrews and Egyptians cannot eat together.
The covenant family and the host nation are divided by table customs.
The Cup that brings all the earth to Egypt for grain still cannot bring Egyptians and Hebrews to the same table.
Not yet.
The division is cultural, not chosen by Joseph.
But it stands, the barrier between the covenant and the world,
even at the table of the one who bridges them.
They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright,
and the youngest according to his youth.
And the men marveled with one another.
Seated in order.
The brothers sit by birthright, oldest to youngest.
The exact order of their births.
How does this Egyptian know?
How does the man who sells grain know who is the firstborn and who is the youngest?
The brothers marvel.
The recognition pattern flickers,
they see something unusual but do not yet see what it means.
The Cup of testing is held by a man who knows them better than they know themselves.
He sent portions to them from before him.
But Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs.
Five times.
The favoritism pattern.
Jacob gave Joseph the coat, one son favored above the others.
Now Joseph favors Benjamin, five times the portion.
The same pattern.
The same Cup.
Joseph repeats the father's favoritism, but as a test.
Will the brothers hate Benjamin the way they hated Joseph?
Will they resent the favored one?
Will they repeat chapter thirty-seven?
Will the coat of many colors become five portions of food?
Will the jealousy that drove them to sell a brother now drive them to harm another?
They drank, and were merry with him.
They drank.
They were merry.
For the first time,
the brothers sit at a table with the one they wronged,
and they do not know it.
The Cup of testing is becoming the Cup of a meal.
Not yet communion, they do not know who he is.
But the bread is set.
The order is given.
The weeping has happened behind the curtain.
And the brothers who could not speak peaceably to Joseph now drink and are merry with him.
The Cup shifts.
The testing is not over, the silver cup is still coming,
the accusation is still coming, the final test is still ahead.
But for this moment, at this table,
the brothers who sold and the brother who was sold sit together.
The dreamer and the dream-breakers eat bread.
The favorite and the envious drink wine.
And the only one who knows is the one who wept in the other room.
Judah's journey reaches its turning point.
Chapter thirty-seven: sell him.
Chapter thirty-eight: she is more righteous than I.
Chapter forty-three: I will bear the blame forever.
The betrayer becomes the surety.
The covenant line through Judah, through Perez, through David, through Christ,
is being prepared by this:
a man who sold his brother now offering himself for a brother.
The Cup that was held by a betrayer is now held by a guarantor.
The vessel is not clean.
But it is changing.
And Jacob, the father who said all these things are against me,
opened his hand.
El Shaddai give you mercy.
If I am bereaved, I am bereaved.
The Cup of yielding.
The surrender that makes everything else possible.
The father who held too tight now lets go.
And the son he let go of stands in a room in Egypt,
looking at the brother who is the son of his mother,
weeping behind a closed door,
preparing to set bread before the men who sold him.
The Cup holds.
The table is set.
The meal is served.
And the testing is almost over.
